title: 'Code blue' training aims to save lives at Vancouver Jail
article: Staff at the Vancouver Jail is undergoing emergency health training to help employees respond should a prisoner be found in a life-threatening situation.
The training in CPR and first aid was one of the recommendations of a coroner's inquest in 2016 into the death of Cheryl Ann Cowan.
Rockdoc Consulting, in collaboration with the Vancouver Police Department, has developed training scenarios for four teams of jail staff, including guards, police, nurses and physicians.
Vancouver police media relations officer Const. Jason Doucette said part of the training includes observing people put into a "code blue" or emergency situation to see how they respond.
"We're really interested in making things better," he said. "Anyone who could be involved in responding to someone's well-being will be taking this training. If you work there, you're taking it."
The last of the four sessions take place Monday.
The five-person coroner's jury determined Cowan died of a brain injury from lack of oxygen caused by a heart attack. Hypothermia and chronic alcoholism were identified as contributing factors.
Cowan, 58, was a mother of two sons. She taught at the private York House School, but ended up an alcoholic and homeless.

Early in morning of Dec. 15, 2014, she was picked up at her estranged husband's home in Dunbar. Although appearing intoxicated, she was able to walk into a police transport van that took her to jail. When police opened the door 48 minutes later, Cowan was unresponsive.

In a video shown to the jury, the van driver, guards, two nurses and a doctor were seen tending her, but none of them performed CPR or used a defibrillator until paramedics arrived 11 minutes later, according to a timeline in an Independent Investigations Office report that cleared the van driver of any wrongdoing.
Cowan was resuscitated, but never fully recovered. She died eight days later.
The coroner also recommended that Vancouver police install video cameras in vehicles used to transport prisoners.
